hints.title: Compare heights, then gradients
hints.body: First write what increasing tells you about the two endpoint heights. To test the first-derivative claim, draw the rising part of a downward-opening quadratic, with short tangents at both endpoints. Compare the heights and gradients separately.
hints.recap: The derivative gives the slope of the graph.
hints.pitfall: Check that your chosen polynomial is increasing throughout your whole interval.
hints.pause: Differentiate your quadratic, choose a suitable interval, and compare the endpoint gradients.

recall.reminder: Differentiate each power term to find the gradient function.

hints.title: Try a cubic for the second derivative
hints.body: Try p(x)=3x−x3. Differentiate twice and choose an interval of positive inputs where the polynomial is increasing.
hints.recap: A function example must satisfy the original condition across the whole interval.
hints.pitfall: Checking only endpoint heights does not prove increase throughout the interval.
hints.pause: Verify your interval using the first derivative, then compare the second derivative at its endpoints.

recall.reminder: A function counterexample must satisfy the original condition across the whole interval.

solution:
1. I is necessary. Increasing p has p(a)≤p(b).

2. II need not hold. For p(x)=9−x2 on [−3,0], p′(x)=−2x≥0. Yet p′(−3)=6>0=p′(0).

3. III need not hold. For p(x)=3x−x3 on [0,1], p′(x)=3−3x2≥0, but p′′(0)=0>−6=p′′(1).

Answer B: I only. Each counterexample is increasing on its entire stated interval.
knowledgePattern: Separate increasing function values from monotonicity of derivatives
